Proem

Learning Goals

Upon the completion of this chapter, the student shall be able to define the state, the nation, and the nation-state; to explain the effects of globalization upon sovereign powers; to identify those institutions which govern the relations of nations; and to distinguish the doctrine of internationalism from that of globalism.

I.

Define

State, nation, and nation-states — understanding their foundational distinctions in political theory.

II.

Explain

The effects of globalization on states and the evolving nature of sovereignty in the modern world.

III.

Identify

The institutions that govern international relations and the actors that shape global affairs.

IV.

Differentiate

Internationalism from globalism, and understand the divergent implications of each doctrine.

⚜ ✦ ⚜
Article The First

The Interstate System

On the Nature of the State

The state hath long been recognised as the fundamental actor in global politics. A nation or territory considered to be politically organised under one government, each state is expected to maintain unchallengeable authority within its borders by virtue of its possessed sovereignty. The modern world-system is structured politically as an interstate system — a system of competing and allying states, described by scholars as "a system of unequally powerful and competing states in which no single state is capable of imposing control on all others."

In time, states began to interact with other states and institutions beyond their territorial boundaries, driven by factors demanding cooperation and interdependence. The study of decisions and interactions across state borders is what scholars call international relations — encompassing military, diplomatic, and strategic dimensions whose nature hath changed significantly under globalization.

Gerardus Mercator's Nova et Aucta Orbis Terrae Descriptio (1569) — among the earliest maps to depict the world's territorial extent, long before the modern sovereign state system took shape.
⚜ The Four Elements of the State — as codified by the Montevideo Convention, 1933
I.

Population

A permanent group of people residing within the territory and subject to the authority of the state.

II.

Territory

A defined geographical area with recognised borders over which the state exercises sovereign control.

III.

Government

An effective, functioning political institution that governs the population and the territory.

IV.

Sovereignty

The supreme authority to govern — internal, within its borders, and external, among other states.

⚜ ✦ ⚜
Article The Second

State, Nation & Nation-State

Distinguishing the Three Concepts

Though the terms are often used interchangeably in common parlance, state, nation, and nation-state represent fundamentally different concepts in the science of politics. A state is a political and legal entity possessing defined territory, a permanent population, an effective government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. It holds a monopoly on the legitimate use of force within its borders. The United Nations currently recognises 193 sovereign states, each with defined governmental structures.

A nation, by contrast, is a cultural and social entity. Political scientist Benedict Anderson defined nations as "imagined communities" — large groups united by shared language, history, culture, traditions, and common aspirations, yet whose members cannot all know one another personally. Importantly, a nation does not require a fixed territory to exist. Before 1948, the Jewish people constituted a nation without a fixed territory of their own.

A nation-state combines both: it is a political entity in which the boundaries of the nation and the state coincide — a single government governs a population sharing a national identity. Examples include Japan and Iceland. Yet true nation-states have grown less common under globalization, as many states contain multiple nations, and many nations remain without states.

The flags of the world's sovereign nations — 193 member states of the United Nations, each a distinct legal entity under international law.
⚜ A Comparative Survey of the Three Concepts

The State

A political and legal entity with defined territory, permanent population, effective government, and sovereignty. The state holds authority over external human actions and is governed by law.

Possession of a definite territory is essential for the state. It is a territorial entity above all.

Examples: The Philippines, France, Brazil, Japan — all 193 UN member states.

The Nation

A cultural and emotional entity — a united body of people bound by common language, religion, history, culture, and political aspirations. It is full of emotional, spiritual, and psychological bonds.

Territory is not essential for a nation. A nation may persist without fixed territory, as love of a common homeland acts as a source of unity.

Examples: The Kurdish people (spanning Turkey, Iraq, Iran & Syria), the Lakota Nation, the Jewish nation before 1948.

The Nation-State

A political entity that combines nation and state — the boundaries of nation and state coincide, with a single government governing a population of shared national identity.

Driven by nationalist sentiment and the principle of self-determination; the ideal form of political organisation under classical nationalism.

Examples: Japan (Japanese nation within Japanese state), Iceland, Portugal — where cultural and political boundaries largely align.
⚜ A Note on Stateless Nations

Some nations exist without a state of their own — these are known as stateless nations. The Kurdish people, spread across Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria, constitute perhaps the most prominent example: a distinct cultural identity without a sovereign state to call its own. Conversely, some states contain multiple nations within their borders — Belgium, with its Flemish and Walloon populations, exemplifies this condition.

Article The Third

State & Sovereignty

Origins of the Modern State

The state emerged in 15th and 16th century Europe as a system of centralised rule that succeeded in subordinating all other institutions and groups. The concept of statehood was attributed to the Peace of Westphalia (1648) — a package of treaties ending the Thirty Years' War — in which Europe's rulers recognised each other's right to govern their own territories free from outside interference. The Westphalian system thus established three enduring principles: state sovereignty, territorial integrity, and non-interference in the domestic affairs of other states.

It is worth noting that throughout world history, there have been repeated attempts to violate these principles — states invading other states, territories being seized by force. These attempts resulted in wars. Nevertheless, the state system persists unto this day as the primary framework for organising the world politically.

The Ratification of the Peace of Westphalia (1648) — establishing state sovereignty, territorial integrity, and non-interference, still governing the modern world order.
⚜ A Chronicle of Sovereign History
1618 — 1648

The Thirty Years' War

A devastating European conflict, concluded by the Peace of Westphalia, establishing the enduring principles of sovereign equality, territorial integrity, and non-interference among the rulers of Europe.

1789

The French Revolution & the Napoleonic Challenge

Napoleon Bonaparte challenged the Westphalian order with principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity, seeking to propagate the ideals of the French Revolution throughout Europe. His defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815 revived the old sovereign order.

August Friedrich Andreas Campe — The Congress of Vienna (1815). The great powers of Europe assembled to restore the Westphalian order after Napoleon's defeat.
1815

The Concert of Europe

Austria, Russia, Prussia, and the United Kingdom formed an alliance of great powers, restoring and stabilising the Westphalian system and establishing a balance-of-power order across the continent.

President Woodrow Wilson (1856–1924) — architect of the Fourteen Points and the principle of national self-determination.
1918

Wilson's Fourteen Points

President Woodrow Wilson proposed European reconstruction anchored in the principle of national self-determination, wherein nations should achieve statehood based on the will of their peoples. This catalysed the construction of modern nation-states.

1933

The Montevideo Convention

Codified the four qualifying elements of statehood: defined territory, permanent population, effective government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.

1945

The United Nations Charter

Established the United Nations as the principal framework for international relations, guaranteeing the sovereign equality of all member states and providing mechanisms for the peaceful resolution of disputes.

⚜ Scholarly Authority — Heywood, 2011

"While internal sovereignty refers to the state's supreme authority within its borders, external sovereignty defines the relationship of states to other states and international actors — establishing the state's capacity to act as an independent and autonomous entity in world affairs."

— Heywood (2011)

Article The Fourth

State & Globalization

On the Nature of Globalization

Globalization is defined as the "widening, intensifying, speeding up, and growing impact of worldwide interconnectedness" — Held and McGrew, 1999. It is more than growing connections between states; it represents a fundamental shift toward the world as a shared social space, wherein local events may diffuse rapidly across all regions of the globe. States are, in a manner of speaking, major facilitators of globalization — through colonisation, trade, the control of domestic affairs, and the conduct of international relations.

It is also a process of deterritorialization: social, political, and economic activities are increasingly stretched across the globe, rendering geography and distance of relative significance. Terrorist and criminal networks operate both locally and globally; national economic space is no longer equivalent with national territorial space. Before globalization, the economy was constrained within the borders of the state's territory; today, national economies have been integrated into a single global market economy — such that economic problems at the global level become problems at the local level.

⚜ Scholarly Authority — Baylis et al., 2011

"A historical process involving a fundamental shift or transformation in the spatial scale of human social organisation that links distant communities and expands the reach of power across regions and continents."

— Baylis et al. (2011)
⚜ Internationalization versus Globalization — A Distinction

Internationalization

  • ◆Growing interdependence between states
  • ◆States remain discrete national units
  • ◆Clearly demarcated national borders
  • ◆Domestic and external remain distinct
  • ◆Sovereignty largely preserved

Globalization

  • ◆Domestic and external distinction dissolves
  • ◆Distance and time rendered irrelevant
  • ◆Local events diffuse rapidly worldwide
  • ◆Power operates transnationally
  • ◆Deterritorialization of social life
⚜ ✦ ⚜
Article The Fifth

Shifting to Global Politics

From International to Global

The term "international relations" was coined by Jeremy Bentham, the British philosopher and legal reformer, in his Principles of Morals and Legislation of 1789. The origins of the modern interstate system are drawn from the Peace of Westphalia, with sovereignty as its fundamental organising principle. Yet this conventional understanding is shifting under the weight of globalization.

In political terms, globalization hath called into question the continued relevance of the Westphalian conception of the nation-state. Due to the interconnectedness of the global system, nation-states have little choice but to work together to deal with cross-border issues such as terrorism, security, climate change, and the movement of refugees. Even the most powerful states must now co-operate with other actors to achieve their aims.

Today, challenges such as terrorism and climate change have acquired a genuinely global character — affecting all states, transcending borders, and requiring coordinated responses beyond traditional state-to-state diplomacy. One country's scale and scope are inherently limited in addressing regional and global issues such as cybercrimes, the global financial crisis, and territorial disputes.

Jacques-Louis David — The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries (1812). Napoleon's challenge to the Westphalian order proved the greatest test of the state system in early modern history.

Article The Sixth

Institutions Governing International Relations

On International Organisations and Global Governance

As the governance of local and international relations hath grown beyond the capacity of national governments alone, a network of international institutions hath emerged to coordinate the interactions of states. Global governance refers to this network of international institutions and organisations that states have created to manage common problems at the international level through cooperation among states, international bodies, and non-state actors alike.

The increase in the number of international organisations and the expansion of their functions have undeniably restricted individual states' sovereignty to a certain extent. Yet this restriction is accepted as the necessary cost of collective action in an interconnected world — for no single country possesses the scale or scope to address regional and global issues such as climate change, cybercrimes, global financial crises, and territorial disputes in isolation.

The United Nations General Assembly Hall, New York — principal forum for all 193 sovereign member states, embodying the principle of sovereign equality.
⚜ Principal International Organisations
UN
United Nations

Founded in 1945, the UN is the foremost intergovernmental organisation, bringing together 193 member states to maintain international peace and security, develop friendly relations among nations, and promote social progress and human rights. Its principal bodies include the Security Council, the General Assembly, and the International Court of Justice.

IMF
International Monetary Fund

The IMF looks to the stability of the international monetary system by monitoring the global economy, lending to countries in financial difficulty, and providing policy and technical advisory functions. It promotes international monetary cooperation, exchange rate stability, and orderly exchange arrangements among its member states.

WTO
World Trade Organization

The WTO is the primary international organisation governing global trade relations. It regulates international trade, ensures the smooth flow of commerce, provides a forum for the negotiation of trade agreements among countries, and operates a dispute settlement mechanism to resolve trade conflicts. Its core principles include non-discrimination, reciprocity, and transparency.

WHO
World Health Organization

The WHO coordinates global responses to pandemics and health crises, sets international health standards, and provides technical guidance to member states. It serves as the directing and coordinating authority on international public health, addressing issues from infectious disease to mental health and universal health coverage.

WB
World Bank

The World Bank provides financial and technical assistance to developing countries for development projects and programmes, with the aim of reducing poverty and supporting long-term economic development. It proclaims free-market principles and discourages excessive state intervention as a development strategy.

NATO
North Atlantic Treaty Org.

A military alliance of Western nations established in 1949, NATO manages collective defence and security among its member states. Together with the UN Security Council, it plays a central role in managing conflicts and maintaining international peace, particularly in the Euro-Atlantic region.

⚜ Regional Organisations
EU
European Union

A political and economic union of 27 member states in Europe, the EU represents perhaps the most advanced experiment in regional integration in the world. It promotes political stability, economic cooperation, and shared governance among its members, pooling sovereignty in key areas.

AU
African Union

The African Union promotes continental unity, solidarity, and cooperation among the states of Africa. It addresses issues of governance, peace and security, and economic development across the continent, and advocates for Africa's interests in the global arena.

ASEAN
Assoc. of Southeast Asian Nations

Established in 1967, ASEAN promotes regional cooperation in Southeast Asia across political, economic, security, and sociocultural dimensions. It operates on the principles of non-interference and consensus among its ten member states, of which the Philippines is a founding member.

ICC
International Criminal Court

The ICC is the first permanent international criminal tribunal, established to prosecute individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression. It represents a landmark development in international law and the global protection of human rights.

⚜ Economic Integration under Globalization
⚜

Global Market Economy

National economies have been integrated into a single global market. Economic problems at the global level — such as the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic — immediately become problems at the local level, demonstrating how thoroughly economic sovereignty hath been transformed.

⚜

Neoliberalism & Economic Sovereignty

Economic interdependence and neoliberal pressures have reduced governments' economic sovereignty, compelling states to adopt free-market policies. Critics, including many NGOs, argue that institutions like the IMF and WTO have at times promoted policies that exacerbate inequality and environmental degradation.

⚜

Multinational Corporations

States are especially threatened by global economic flows dominated by multinational corporations, whose operations transcend national borders and whose revenues may rival those of sovereign states. UK companies with overseas headquarters exemplify how national economic space no longer corresponds to territorial space.

⚜ ✦ ⚜
Article The Seventh

New Actors on the World Stage

Beyond the Nation-State

Under globalization, power is increasingly organised on a transregional, transnational, or transcontinental basis. Many actors — from international organisations to criminal networks — exercise power from within, across, and against states in an increasingly interconnected global system. Aside from governments, non-state actors continue to increase their roles in global governance, and the expansion of their functions hath undeniably restricted individual states' sovereignty to a certain extent.

This relative denationalization of power means the nation-state may no longer hold an unchallenged monopoly on power resources. The rise of new actors — empowered further by social media and transnational advocacy networks — fundamentally changes who participates in the conduct of global affairs and whose voice is heard upon the world stage.

🌐

International Organisations

The UN, WTO, WHO — intergovernmental bodies whose expanded functions govern global affairs and constrain state sovereignty.

🏛

Multinational Corporations

Enterprises operating across borders with economic reach rivalling sovereign states, reshaping national economic policies.

🤝

NGOs & Civil Society

Non-governmental organisations and interest groups advocating across national borders and shaping global norms.

⚔

Terrorist Networks

Operating both locally and globally, these networks challenge state authority, security, and the principle of territorial sovereignty.

🌿

Environmental Groups

Transnational advocates for global climate governance, holding states and corporations accountable across borders.

📜

Media & Technology

Shaping public opinion, enabling transnational activism, and diffusing information — and misinformation — far beyond national borders.

The Trend Towards Global Governance

The growing number of complex political issues — terrorism, climate change, pandemics, global financial crises — hath led states to seek collective, coordinated responses through multilateral frameworks involving both state and non-state actors alike. Global governance collectively manages common problems at the international level, as these transnational challenges transcend national borders and cannot be effectively addressed by any single nation.

The United Nations serves as the principal venue for convening member states, guaranteeing equal participation in international relations according to the principle of sovereign equality — even as globalization continues to challenge the very foundations upon which that sovereignty rests. The increased relevance of international organisations at both the global (the UN, NATO, ICC) and regional (EU, AU, ASEAN) levels makes manifest the new reality of an interconnected world order.
